title: Failed sign-ins are bounded, per name and per address
description: Nothing bounds failed sign-ins today (the user policy reports LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout -1). D-016 opens the API to any origin, so on a private-network server a web page in a viewer's browser could guess names and passwords and read the answers; servers on the internet are exposed to guessing already.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first: what Jellyfin 12.4 does after failed sign-ins (its LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout, what a locked account answers) and what jellyfin-web shows for 401, 403, 429 and 503 on sign-in, recorded in compat/captures

Per name (D-020): after 20 failed sign-ins for one name within 15 minutes, from devices that have not signed in to that account before, any number of addresses and replicas, further such sign-ins for it are refused for 15 minutes; a refused attempt checks no password and counts as no failure; a right password during the refusal is refused the same way, and signs in afterwards; no success resets a count and no account is ever disabled by failures; shown with real processes

Known devices (D-020): a device (DeviceId) that held a token for the account within the last 30 days is outside the per-name bound and has its own count for that account, 10 failures within 15 minutes then refused for 15 minutes; with the name refused to strangers under guessing from many addresses, its owner signs in from such a device at the first try, shown by a test; a guesser sending that DeviceId gets no more than that device's count

Per address (D-020, D-022): with proxies declared or `trustedProxies: []`, 10 failed sign-ins within 15 minutes from one address across all names refuse that address for 15 minutes, whatever the name or device, and a success on one account resets nothing; an IPv6 address counts as its /64; one address alone never causes a name to be refused to others, shown by a test (10 failures on one name from one address, then its owner signs in from another address on a new device). The address of a request from a declared proxy is the rightmost X-Forwarded-For entry that is not a declared proxy, and no other entry: when the header is missing, every entry is a declared proxy, or that entry does not parse, the per-address bound is not applied to that request (it neither counts nor is refused per address; the per-name and known-device bounds apply), and a declared proxy's own address is never counted or refused, shown by a test (11 failed sign-ins through a declared proxy with no usable entry, then a right password by the same path signs in). A client behind a declared proxy that appends to the header cannot get itself uncounted or counted as another address by anything it sends (no header, an unparseable one, one naming the proxy's address or another client's), shown by a test
A viewer who mistypes 9 times in a row and then types the right password signs in; every route that takes a password is bounded the same way
The bounds hold under parallel attempts: 200 sign-ins at once for one name, spread over two api replicas, check no more than 20 passwords; shown with two replicas as separate processes

A refusal answers 403 with a Retry-After header in whole seconds until it ends, readable by a cross-origin page (D-016, D-020); it is the same status, body and headers for a name that exists and one that does not (D-014), and an unknown name counts toward the per-name bound exactly as a real one

Unknown names are remembered within a fixed bound stated in docs/access.md; a flood of invented names (100,000 in a test) neither changes nor drops a real account's count, nor makes any unknown name answer differently from a real one at the same count (D-020)

Before any bound, a wrong password and an unknown name answer alike and do the same password work, so the time taken does not tell them apart; shown by a check that can fail (Jellyfin 12.4 was observed at 1 ms against 77 ms)

docs/access.md states the three bounds, how long each lasts, the worst-case guesses per account per day (1,920, plus 960 per known DeviceId the guesser holds), and the longest a viewer with the right password is kept out by someone else's guesses: none on a device that has signed in before; on a new device until 15 minutes after the guessing stops, with Quick Connect named as the way around once built; a check holds each number

Each refusal is logged with which bound refused, an address, and the account name only when the account exists (an unknown name's text is never logged, since viewers type passwords into the name box), never the password. The line itself says what its address is (D-023): the address the per-address bound counted, or, when none was attributed to the request (`trustedProxies` absent, or a declared proxy with no usable forwarded entry), the peer's, under a field name that says it is the peer. In that second case the line also carries the X-Forwarded-For header as the peer sent it, marked as unverified, quoted, cut to 256 bytes and with control characters escaped, and left out when no header came. That value never counts toward a bound, never decides a refusal and is never a metric label, shown by a test. Shown through the shipped compose stack itself, not a stand-in peer: a refused sign-in there is logged, and docs/running.md states what each field of that line held in the run and whether either is the client's own address. If neither is, docs/running.md says that in that stack the line identifies the account and the bound but not the client, that the peer's address is every viewer's and must never be blocked, and that the client's address is known only to whatever stands in front of the stack. Refusals are counted in a metric labelled by bound only, and failed sign-ins in another, neither with an account or address label; docs/running.md names both for alerting, and nowhere says the line names the client's address without saying when it does.

docs/running.md says which address counts behind an ingress, and how an operator confirms before declaring that the counted address is each client's own (a failed sign-in from two devices shows two addresses) and what follows if it is not (one guesser or mistyping viewer refuses everyone behind that address for 15 minutes); the operator declares `trustedProxies`; a forwarded header from any other peer is ignored, shown by a test; with the key absent the per-address bound is off, the per-name bounds hold, a warning naming the key is logged at every start-up and a metric says the bound is off (D-020); with `[]` declared, a forwarded header arriving from a private peer is logged once per process as a likely undeclared ingress; a sign-in from a declared proxy with no usable forwarded entry is logged once per process as a warning naming `trustedProxies`, and each one is counted in a metric with no address or account label, named in docs/running.md for alerting (D-022). The shipped compose stack leaves `trustedProxies` absent (D-022), because every client reaches its ingress from the Docker bridge gateway's address: its compose file carries the key commented out with when to declare it, docs/running.md says the per-address bound is off in that stack and why and that the per-name and known-device bounds hold, and on the stack as shipped ten wrong passwords for ten invented names from the host followed by the administrator's right password from a new device signs in, shown by a check that can fail docs/running.md also says (D-023): how to give a declared ingress an address that survives its container being recreated (or to declare its network's prefix), and the compose file's comment points to that paragraph; that a server with no ingress declares `trustedProxies: []` so the peer counts and the start-up warning stops; that viewers behind one household NAT share one counted address; and that a forwarded entry must be a bare address, since one written with a port or brackets is treated as unusable and the per-address bound is not applied to that request.
A token already issued keeps working while its account or address is refused: a playing film, its progress reports and the account's other devices are unaffected, shown by a test

On jellyfin-web a refused sign-in shows the 403 text ('not authorized… at this time… contact your server administrator'), recorded from a run against the build; docs/access.md says this is what viewers read and that the administrator finds the reason in the log and metric (D-020: jellyfin-web has no 'try again later'). What Fluster shows is recorded in JS-075 (D-019)

LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout reports -1 for every user; compat/differences.yaml lists that jellyscale refuses temporarily per name and address where Jellyfin has no bound by default, and that a set value is not honoured (D-020)
notes: D-020: refuse (403 with Retry-After), never slow; criteria 2, 3 and 7 land together: a per-name lock without the known-device allowance does not ship. If refinement finds it too large for one build, bring a split to the product owner.
